core_principles: Perception of effort (RPE) during sustained submaximal isometric leg extensions is dissociated from fatigue-related changes in force or EMG amplitude.
Peak motor unit recruitment of the biceps brachii can be achieved at any workload greater than 60% of 1RM, provided the set is taken to momentary muscular fatigue (MMF).
Exercise intensity is best defined by the proximity to failure (the final repetition) rather than the initial percentage of 1RM.
Adhering to a controlled repetition tempo (e.g., 3-1-3-1 seconds) standardizes muscle activation measurements during resistance training.
Using a weightlifting belt in conjunction with a simultaneous Valsalva maneuver increases intra-abdominal pressure to support the spine during heavy lifts like the deadlift.
common_mistakes: Assuming that lower-intensity training (e.g., 60% 1RM) cannot achieve maximal motor unit recruitment (it can, if taken to momentary muscular fatigue).
Defining training intensity solely by the percentage of 1RM rather than proximity to momentary muscular fatigue (the final repetition).
specific_findings: For sustained isometric leg extensions (knee joint = 120°), mean times to exhaustion were: RPE 2 = 300.0 ± 0.0 s; RPE 5 = 202.0 ± 95.5 s; RPE 8 = 72.7 ± 27.6 s.
The percent decline in force during sustained isometric leg extensions decreased with each increase in RPE: RPE 2 = 61.0 ± 18.5%; RPE 5 = 47.4 ± 19.6%; RPE 8 = 24.9 ± 13.2%.

During biceps curls to momentary muscular fatigue (MMF) with a 3-1-3-1 sec tempo, percent MVC for the concentric portion of the final repetition was 62.5±27.8% at 40% 1RM, 71.7±24.0% at 60% 1RM, 72.8±18.4% at 80% 1RM, and 79.6±18.0% at 100% 1RM.
There was no significant difference (NSD) in peak motor unit recruitment among 60%, 80%, and 100% 1RM biceps curls when performed to momentary muscular fatigue.
Wearing a weightlifting belt generally reports 5-15% greater loading during lifts.
